title: Points, lines, segments, rays, and planes
goal: Explain the principles and solve standard problems involving points, lines, segments, rays, and planes.
concept: A line extends without endpoints; a segment has two endpoints, and a ray has one. Three noncollinear points determine a unique plane.
method: Sketch and label each object before using its length or incidence relationships. Only segments have finite length.
guardrail: Do not interpret a full line or ray as having a finite length.

title: Angle types, measurement, and relationships
goal: Explain the principles and solve standard problems involving angle types, measurement, and relationships.
concept: An acute angle is less than 90°, a right angle is 90°, an obtuse angle is between 90° and 180°, and a straight angle is 180°.
method: For complementary angles use a total of 90°; for supplementary or linear-pair angles use 180°.
guardrail: Do not confuse complementary with supplementary angles.

title: Parallel and perpendicular lines
goal: Explain the principles and solve standard problems involving parallel and perpendicular lines.
concept: Parallel coplanar lines never meet; perpendicular lines intersect at a 90° angle.
method: Use perpendicularity only when the 90° condition is given or follows from an established theorem.
guardrail: Lines that look perpendicular in a schematic may not be.

title: Transversal and corresponding angles
goal: Explain the principles and solve standard problems involving transversal and corresponding angles.
concept: When a transversal crosses parallel lines, corresponding and alternate interior angles are congruent; consecutive interior angles are supplementary.
method: Determine the angle positions before applying a parallel-line theorem.
guardrail: Angle-pair theorems require the two lines to be parallel.

title: Reasoning, postulates, and elementary proofs
goal: Explain the principles and solve standard problems involving reasoning, postulates, and elementary proofs.
concept: Geometric proofs start from defined terms, accepted postulates and already-proven theorems; each deduction needs a reason.
method: Use a two-column or paragraph proof, state the given, and justify every inference.
guardrail: A diagram is not proof of equality, parallelism or congruence.

title: Geometric constructions with compass and straightedge
goal: Explain the principles and solve standard problems involving geometric constructions with compass and straightedge.
concept: A compass constructs equal-radius arcs; an unmarked straightedge draws lines through marked points.
method: A perpendicular bisector is constructed using equal-radius arcs from segment endpoints with a radius exceeding half the segment.
guardrail: An unmarked straightedge cannot directly measure lengths.

title: Triangle classifications and angle sums
goal: Explain the principles and solve standard problems involving triangle classifications and angle sums.
concept: A triangle has an interior angle sum of 180°. It may be classified by sides or by angles.
method: Subtract the known angles from 180° before assigning the triangle class.
guardrail: Two interior angles cannot both be obtuse.

title: Congruent triangles and criteria
goal: Explain the principles and solve standard problems involving congruent triangles and criteria.
concept: Triangles are congruent when they agree in shape and size. Common valid tests are SSS, SAS, ASA, AAS, and RHS/HL under right-triangle conditions.
method: Check corresponding parts and the included-angle requirement for SAS.
guardrail: SSA and AAA do not establish triangle congruence in general.

title: Triangle inequalities and side-angle relationships
goal: Explain the principles and solve standard problems involving triangle inequalities and side-angle relationships.
concept: For a nondegenerate triangle, each side is shorter than the sum and longer than the absolute difference of the other two sides.
method: Evaluate |a−b| < c < a+b before solving construction problems.
guardrail: Equality yields a degenerate triangle, not a proper triangle.

title: Triangle medians, altitudes, and centers
goal: Explain the principles and solve standard problems involving triangle medians, altitudes, and centers.
concept: A median joins a vertex to the opposite midpoint; an altitude is perpendicular to the opposite side line. The centroid divides a median 2:1 from the vertex.
method: Use the ratio vertex-to-centroid : centroid-to-midpoint = 2:1.
guardrail: The orthocenter can lie outside an obtuse triangle.

title: Pythagorean theorem and converse
goal: Explain the principles and solve standard problems involving pythagorean theorem and converse.
concept: In a right triangle, the square of the hypotenuse equals the sum of the squares of the legs. The converse identifies right triangles.
method: Identify the side opposite the right angle before substituting.
guardrail: Never use the Pythagorean equality for a non-right triangle.

title: Special right triangles (30-60-90, 45-45-90)
goal: Explain the principles and solve standard problems involving special right triangles (30-60-90, 45-45-90).
concept: A 45–45–90 triangle has side ratio 1:1:√2; a 30–60–90 triangle has ratio 1:√3:2.
method: Map given side to its role in the ratio before scaling.
guardrail: Do not confuse the side opposite 30° with the longer leg.

title: Triangle similarity criteria and proportions
goal: Explain the principles and solve standard problems involving triangle similarity criteria and proportions.
concept: Similar triangles have equal corresponding angles and proportional corresponding sides. AA, SAS similarity and SSS similarity may establish similarity.
method: List matching vertices in order and write one consistent side ratio.
guardrail: Similarity does not imply equal size or equal area.

title: Proportional segments and midsegment theorem
goal: Explain the principles and solve standard problems involving proportional segments and midsegment theorem.
concept: The midsegment joining two triangle-side midpoints is parallel to the third side and half its length.
method: Check that both endpoints are midpoints; then use the one-half ratio.
guardrail: A line through only one midpoint is not necessarily a midsegment.

title: Right-triangle trigonometric ratios and applications
goal: Explain the principles and solve standard problems involving right-triangle trigonometric ratios and applications.
concept: For acute angles in a right triangle, sin θ = opposite/hypotenuse, cos θ = adjacent/hypotenuse and tan θ = opposite/adjacent.
method: Convert the given angle to degrees before using trigonometric functions when appropriate.
guardrail: The standard ratios assume a right triangle and correctly identified reference angle.

title: Heron formula and area from three sides
goal: Explain the principles and solve standard problems involving heron formula and area from three sides.
concept: Heron’s formula finds triangle area from three side lengths without measuring an altitude.
method: Compute semiperimeter s=(a+b+c)/2, then A=√[s(s−a)(s−b)(s−c)].
guardrail: Sides must satisfy strict triangle inequalities.

title: Parallelograms and trapezoids
goal: Explain the principles and solve standard problems involving parallelograms and trapezoids.
concept: A parallelogram has opposite sides parallel; a trapezoid has at least one pair of parallel sides under the inclusive definition used here.
method: Identify parallel bases and perpendicular height before using area relationships.
guardrail: Textbooks vary on whether a trapezoid has exactly one or at least one parallel pair; state the convention.

title: Rectangles, squares, rhombi, and kites
goal: Explain the principles and solve standard problems involving rectangles, squares, rhombi, and kites.
concept: A rectangle has four right angles; a square has four equal sides and four right angles; a rhombus has four equal sides; a kite has two pairs of adjacent equal sides.
method: Use diagonals when a kite or rhombus area is given by one-half their product.
guardrail: The kite diagonal-area rule requires perpendicular diagonals; ordinary convex kites satisfy it.

title: Properties of regular polygons
goal: Explain the principles and solve standard problems involving properties of regular polygons.
concept: A regular polygon has equal side lengths and equal interior angles; its center-to-side perpendicular is the apothem.
method: Use central angle 360°/n and interior angle 180°−360°/n for regular n-gons.
guardrail: A polygon with only equal angles is not necessarily regular.

title: Polygon angles and number of diagonals
goal: Explain the principles and solve standard problems involving polygon angles and number of diagonals.
concept: For n-sided polygons, interior angles sum to (n−2)180°; a convex n-gon has n(n−3)/2 diagonals.
method: Count diagonals by choosing nonadjacent vertex pairs and divide by two for duplicate directions.
guardrail: These formulas assume a simple polygon with n≥3.

title: Perimeter and area of triangles
goal: Explain the principles and solve standard problems involving perimeter and area of triangles.
concept: Triangle area is one-half base times its perpendicular height; perimeter is the sum of side lengths.
method: Use the corresponding altitude even for obtuse triangles, where it may fall outside the base segment.
guardrail: A slanted side is not automatically the perpendicular height.

title: Areas of quadrilaterals and trapezoids
goal: Explain the principles and solve standard problems involving areas of quadrilaterals and trapezoids.
concept: A trapezoid area is one-half the sum of parallel bases times their perpendicular separation.
method: Use arithmetic mean of the two bases, then multiply by the perpendicular height.
guardrail: Nonparallel side lengths must not be substituted for the height.

title: Areas of regular polygons and apothems
goal: Explain the principles and solve standard problems involving areas of regular polygons and apothems.
concept: A regular polygon can be divided into congruent triangles from its center; total area equals one-half perimeter times apothem.
method: Find the full perimeter before multiplying by the apothem.
guardrail: Formula A=Pa/2 assumes the apothem of a tangential regular polygon.

title: Composite plane figures and removed regions
goal: Explain the principles and solve standard problems involving composite plane figures and removed regions.
concept: Composite-area problems use the sum of nonoverlapping pieces minus cutouts or holes.
method: Draw a decomposition map; identify hidden overlaps and shared boundaries before summing.
guardrail: Perimeter needs a separate boundary trace; area subtraction alone does not give perimeter.

title: Similarity scaling: perimeters and areas
goal: Explain the principles and solve standard problems involving similarity scaling: perimeters and areas.
concept: Under similarity with linear scale k, perimeter scales by k and area by k².
method: Square the linear ratio before applying to an area comparison.
guardrail: A ratio of areas must not be used directly as the side ratio.

title: Circle vocabulary, chords, diameters, and tangents
goal: Explain the principles and solve standard problems involving circle vocabulary, chords, diameters, and tangents.
concept: A circle is the set of points at fixed radius from a center; a chord joins circle points and a diameter is a chord through the center.
method: For a tangent point, draw a radius perpendicular to the tangent line.
guardrail: A secant passes through two circle points; a tangent touches at exactly one point.

title: Central angles, arc length, and circumference
goal: Explain the principles and solve standard problems involving central angles, arc length, and circumference.
concept: The circumference of a circle is 2πr. An arc subtended by central angle θ is a θ/360 fraction of the circumference.
method: Use degrees consistently in the fraction θ/360.
guardrail: If the angle is supplied in radians, use L=rθ instead.

title: Inscribed angles, secants, and intersecting chords
goal: Explain the principles and solve standard problems involving inscribed angles, secants, and intersecting chords.
concept: An inscribed angle is half its intercepted arc measure. Intersecting chords inside a circle create an angle equal to half the sum of their intercepted arcs.
method: For chord lengths, use the intersecting-chords product equality.
guardrail: The half-arc theorem requires the vertex on the circle; interior intersection uses an arc sum.

title: Circle sectors and circular segments
goal: Explain the principles and solve standard problems involving circle sectors and circular segments.
concept: A circular sector has area proportional to its central angle. A circular segment area equals the sector minus the corresponding triangular wedge for a minor segment.
method: Calculate segment areas with the angle in radians in the radian-based formula.
guardrail: The sector-minus-triangle expression is for the minor segment when 0°<θ≤180°.

title: Tangency, secant lengths, and chord properties
goal: Explain the principles and solve standard problems involving tangency, secant lengths, and chord properties.
concept: Tangents from one exterior point have equal lengths. For a tangent segment PT to a circle of center O, triangle OPT is right.
method: Use power of a point and the tangent–radius right triangle only when the point lies outside the circle.
guardrail: For tangent length, external point distance must exceed radius.

title: Cyclic quadrilaterals and Ptolemy theorem
goal: Explain the principles and solve standard problems involving cyclic quadrilaterals and ptolemy theorem.
concept: Opposite angles in a cyclic quadrilateral sum to 180°. Ptolemy’s theorem relates its two diagonals and opposite side products.
method: Use Ptolemy only after verifying all four vertices lie on one circle.
guardrail: Not every quadrilateral is cyclic.

title: Inscribed and circumscribed polygons
goal: Explain the principles and solve standard problems involving inscribed and circumscribed polygons.
concept: An inscribed polygon has vertices on the circle. A circumscribed regular polygon has sides tangent to an incircle.
method: Relate regular polygon side length to circumradius or apothem using the central right triangle.
guardrail: For a regular n-gon, side and apothem formulas must use the same n and circle.

title: Loci and geometric constructions
goal: Explain the principles and solve standard problems involving loci and geometric constructions.
concept: A locus is the set of all points satisfying a geometric condition, such as fixed distance from a point or equal distance from two points.
method: Translate each condition into a geometric construction: circle, perpendicular bisector, or angle bisector.
guardrail: A construction solves only the stated conditions; an extra constraint may eliminate some points.

title: Translations, rotations, reflections, dilations
goal: Explain the principles and solve standard problems involving translations, rotations, reflections, dilations.
concept: Rigid motions (translations, rotations and reflections) preserve lengths and angles. Dilations preserve angles and scale lengths by |k|.
method: Use coordinates or congruent triangles to test invariants under each transformation.
guardrail: A dilation with scale other than ±1 does not preserve area.

title: Surveying-style distances and indirect measurements
goal: Explain the principles and solve standard problems involving surveying-style distances and indirect measurements.
concept: Indirect measurement models use similar triangles or right-triangle trigonometry. Field measurements must include units, instrument offsets and reference angles.
method: For similar triangles, pair equal angle vertices and comparable side lengths before cross-multiplication.
guardrail: Sloping-ground distances cannot be substituted for horizontal distances without adjustment.
